messages.content: You coach a learner of English (their own language is Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China)) who is rewriting part of a real post before publishing it. Two people talk to them: a reader from the community, who speaks English and reacts like a real person in the thread, and a tutor, who speaks Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) and addresses the learner informally, as a friendly tutor would. The writer may write to you in any language; whatever they write in, everything you write for them is in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China).

Where it will be posted: AO3 (“Long Way Home”, Chapter 24: The Moonstone). Readers: mossfur_writes, the author; lichenpaw, another reader.
The writer's note about it, in their words: Warriors is a series of novels about clans of wild cats. Bluestar, a clan leader, once loved Oakheart of a rival clan; this fic retells her last journey to the Moonstone, where leaders meet the spirits of their ancestors.
Title: Comment on a fic you loved
The post so far:
<<<
I read this fic since the first chapter and the ending made me cry. The scene when Bluestar didn't look back at the camp is staying with me, because she choose to go alone even though she's scared.

* * *

I think it's more about what she find. The journey she did many times, but this time maybe StarClan will tell her Oakheart isn't waiting for her. That's why she makes herself stop thinking of him, I think.
>>>
The spot: "The scene when Bluestar didn't look back at the camp is staying with me, because she choose to go alone even though she's scared." in The scene when Bluestar didn't look back at the camp is staying with me, because she choose to go alone even though she's scared.
What is wrong there: 英语读者看到"scared"后通常会期待说明害怕的对象，而这里紧接"go alone"，很容易理解为害怕独自上路。句子没有给出害怕的具体对象，所以读者无法确定作者所指的恐惧，只能再追问。
What the writer means (confirmed by them): 她害怕在月石上得知奥克心已不再等她
The learner will now write this part themselves in English. Prepare everything the session needs, in this order:
- reader: what the reader says on reaching this spot as it stands: one short line in English (at most 15 words), in character (puzzled, curious, teasing; never a teacher). The reader cannot read Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China): an untranslated passage is simply a gap to them, so react to what is missing and never mention the other language.
- replaces: exactly "The scene when Bluestar didn't look back at the camp is staying with me, because she choose to go alone even though she's scared.", copied character for character (the text around it is someone else's business). ref must fit in its place.
- keep: every point, detail, question, hedge and feeling in replaces, as short English notes, in order. The reference must carry each one unless the writer's meaning above drops it.
- ref: the reference version: what a fluent member of this community would write here to say exactly what the writer means, in the writer's voice and register. Keep everything the writer already says that still serves this meaning (their evidence, their reasoning, their own words) and add only what is missing. Never invent facts the writer has not given, here or in what they told you: no scene, event, line or detail from a work, no names, numbers, dates, quotes or personal circumstances. Where the meaning needs one (the evidence, which scene, what happened to them), write a short placeholder in its place, in English, between ⟨ and ⟩ (for example ⟨the scene you mean⟩), and the writer will fill it in. Where the problem is how the sentence is built (order, emphasis, angle, nominalisation), rebuild it the way this community would say it; do not stop at the smallest fix. Keep the strength the writer confirmed: where the problem is how something lands on its reader (too pushy, too blunt) and the writer means a firm need, a request or a demand, say it the way this place says such things politely and keep it firm; never turn it into something optional or a passing wish. Where the writer reached for an image or a joke, use this community's own equivalent if it has one rather than flattening it into plain words. Where the writer built a figure on purpose (a parallel or echo, a deliberate repetition, wordplay), ref keeps the figure and only puts natural words into it; the why note for such a word says the figure works and why the word changes. ref never says again what the post already says right before or after the replaced text (a reason or detail the next sentence gives stays there). ref replaces exactly the replaces text and carries every keep note and every name, title or label in it (a dish's name before its description, a person's name); it is the final text for that span: anything else wrong or unnatural inside it is fixed too, even where it is the writer's own wording. The writer's voice stays: casual spelling and capitalisation (all lowercase, capitals for emphasis, keysmashes, stretched letters, a missing apostrophe in a contraction), slang, emoji and the community's own shorthand, wherever fluent members of this community write that way too; so does a greeting or a word from another language used as flavour that readers will get. Names (characters, people, usernames, places, the community's terms) are the writer's: leave how they spell and capitalise them and which name they use, unless a reader could not tell who is meant. None of these is a problem in either pass. But wording carried over from Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) (a calque, a collocation, structure or set phrase a fluent writer would not produce) is not voice: it is a problem however casual the post. ref keeps that voice. Put [square brackets] around two to four single words that carry the key choices.
- alts: one or two other natural ways to say it, without brackets.
- pieces: three to eight hint pieces: the content words and short collocations (one to three words) that carry the meaning, including the writer's own words worth reusing. Each piece is English words only: no grammar notes, glosses, symbols or instructions. A piece names a word, never how to use it ("worth", not "worth + -ing" or "worth coming"). Not consecutive chunks of ref, no function-word glue, no full clauses: the learner must still build the sentence. "x / y" offers a fork.
- construct: the one reusable pattern this spot teaches, as a learner would jot it in a notebook: at most eight words, a English frame with one placeholder ("X left him + adjective", "What really got me was …"), optionally a short Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) gloss. Not a grammar formula.
- why: one entry per choice in ref that the learner might not make themselves. label: the English words; note, in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China): why this choice here, contrasted with what the learner wrote or would likely write, with a nuance or a tiny example when it helps. Concrete and specific, never "more natural" or "more appropriate" alone.
- checks: the mistakes this learner is likely to make on a first try, most important first: missing a part of the meaning, a structure carried over from Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China), the specific error already in their draft, a wrong word for this sense. For each: problem (what the grader should look for, in English); reader (optional: how the reader reacts when it happens, one English line in character, only when the meaning really suffers); hint (Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China): a nudge that points at the gap without giving the words); tell (Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China): says the fix plainly, with the words).
- success: the reader's reaction once the learner gets it right: in English, in character, at most 12 words, a reaction to what is now said (not a summary of it).
- prompt: the tutor's instruction in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) to start writing: one short sentence that fits the size of the spot (a clause, a sentence, a passage). The writer has just confirmed what they mean, so do not restate it; never mention punctuation, span boundaries or what comes after; never contain any word or structure from ref.

result.text: {"reader":"Wait, she's scared of the trip? Or of what she'll find?","replaces":"The scene when Bluestar didn't look back at the camp is staying with me, because she choose to go alone even though she's scared.","keep":["The scene when Bluestar didn't look back at the camp: the scene the writer means, named as it is","is staying with me: the scene is still with the writer, a feeling that lingers","because: the reason the scene stays","she choose to go alone: her choice to go alone (fix the verb form)","even though: she goes despite fear","she's scared: the fear, which needs an object (what she is afraid of)"],"ref":"The scene when Bluestar didn't look back at the camp is staying with me, because she [chose] to go alone even though she was [scared] of what she'd [learn] at the Moonstone.","alts":["The scene when Bluestar didn't look back at the camp is staying with me, because she chose to go alone even though she was afraid of what she'd learn at the Moonstone.","The scene when Bluestar didn't look back at the camp is staying with me, because she chose to go alone even though she was afraid of what she'd find at the Moonstone."],"pieces":["chose","scared","learn","Moonstone","alone","afraid"],"construct":"was scared of what + clause（害怕的对象用 of what 引出）","why":[{"label":"scared","note":"scared 后面要接 of 才能说明怕的是什么。原文只写 she's scared，读者会以为她怕独自上路，而作者真正怕的是到了月石才知道的事。这个词本身没错，要补上它的对象。"},{"label":"chose","note":"故事是过去时（didn't look back），所以这里要用过去式 chose。原文 choose 是现在式，和上下文时态不一致。"},{"label":"learn","note":"这里指她在月石上会得知的事，用 learn 比 find 更贴近作者的意思，因为重点是得到的消息，而不是找到东西。下一句会再说明具体是什么，这里只需点出她怕的是得知这件事。"},{"label":"would learn / she'd learn","note":"句子主语在过去时的叙述里，怕的是将来才会知道的事，所以用 would（缩写 'd）表示过去看来的将来。直接写 will 会打断过去时的叙述。"}],"checks":[{"problem":"The sentence must say what she is scared of, not just that she is scared, so the reader does not think the fear is about going alone.","reader":"Scared of what, though? Going alone is scary, sure, but why this trip?","hint":"想想她怕的不是独自走这段路，而是到了那里之后发生的事。","tell":"在 scared 后面用 of what 加一个从句，说明她怕知道什么。"},{"problem":"The verb must match the past tense of the story (didn't look back), so use the past form of choose.","reader":null,"hint":"故事里别的动词都是过去时，choose 这里也要一起变。","tell":"把 choose 改成 chose。"},{"problem":"A Chinese-style structure like 'she is scared of the journey itself' places the fear on the trip instead of on what she will learn.","reader":"Wait, she's scared of the trip? Or of what she'll find?","hint":"害怕的对象要放在 of 后面，并且是她将要知道的事情，不是路上的事。","tell":"不要写 scared of the journey，要写 scared of what she'd learn at the Moonstone，把恐惧放在得知消息上。"},{"problem":"The tense of the fear clause must agree with the story's past tense (she was scared, she'd learn).","reader":null,"hint":"既然叙述是过去时，怕的那一刻和将来才知道的事要一起往前推。","tell":"把 she's scared 改成 she was scared，把 learn 前面加上 would（写成 she'd learn）。"}],"success":"Oh, so she's bracing for the answer itself. That hurts.","prompt":"句子里要点明她到底怕的是什么，别只停在害怕二字上。"}
